title: The history of the iron
tagline: Two thousand years from a pan of hot coals to a solar ironing cart.
intro: People have pressed cloth with heat and weight for at least two thousand years: pans of coals in China, solid sad irons, and charcoal box irons like the istri-wala's. Electricity, the thermostat and steam turned the iron into a precise machine in the twentieth century, while laundries and dhobis pressed with boilers and charcoal. Today care labels, safety standards and new kinds of power shape how we iron.

eras.name: Heat from the fire
eras.summary: Irons are heated in fires or filled with coals. Weight stores the heat; handles get hot.

eras.name: Electric irons
eras.summary: Resistance heaters, a hot point at the tip, and the bimetal thermostat that holds a set temperature.

eras.name: Steam takes over
eras.summary: Laundries press with boiler steam, a steam iron goes on sale in 1926, and India's dhobi ghats press for whole cities.

eras.name: Labels, standards and new power
eras.summary: Care-label dots, compulsory safety marks, and a solar cart to replace the charcoal iron.

events.title: Pans of hot coals smooth cloth
events.text: Metal pans filled with hot coals were used to smooth fabric in China in the 1st century BCE. The pan had a flat bottom and a handle, like a large scoop, and its heat and weight pressed the cloth.
events.why: It is the oldest form of the idea every iron still uses: hot, heavy and flat.

events.title: The sad iron
events.text: Thick, triangular slabs of cast iron with a handle were heated in a fire or on a stove. 'Sad' is an old English word for solid. Laundry workers kept several heating at once and swapped them as they cooled.
events.why: Mass stores heat: the same reason the istri-wala's iron is heavy today.

events.title: Box irons filled with coals
events.text: Later irons were hollow boxes filled with hot coals or a heated metal slug. Some had to be aerated with bellows to keep the coals burning. In Kerala, burning coconut shells were traditionally used in place of charcoal.
events.why: This is the charcoal iron still used on India's streets, revived by a breath of air.

events.title: A cool, detachable handle
events.text: Mary Florence Potts patented a sad iron with a detachable wooden handle (US patent 113,448), after a first patent in 1870. One handle clipped onto several iron bases, so a cooled base could be swapped for a hot one at once.
events.why: It made hot irons safer to hold and ironing faster, and became one of the most popular irons ever made.

events.title: The cold-handled iron goes on show
events.text: Potts's cold-handled sad iron was displayed at the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition. By 1891 machines were mass-producing thousands of her wooden handles a day.
events.why: A small safety idea spread around the world.

events.title: Steam comes to the laundries
events.text: The use of steam became common in commercial laundries in the 1880s, long before it reached household irons.
events.why: Steam, made in a boiler, did the heavy work first in laundries, as it still does in a boiler press.

events.title: The electric flatiron is patented
events.text: Henry W. Seely patented an 'electric flat-iron' (US patent 259,054) with a resistance heater inside, near its face, run from a lighting circuit. It weighed almost 15 pounds (6.8 kg) and took a long time to heat.
events.why: Heat made by current in a resistance is how every electric iron works.

events.title: Mumbai's Dhobi Ghat is built
events.text: The open-air laundry at Mahalaxmi was constructed in 1890. Today over 7,000 people wash, dry and press more than a lakh clothes a day there, for hotels, hospitals and laundries across the city.
events.why: Washing and pressing for a whole city is skilled work done by hand to this day.

events.title: A dhobi ghat for Calcutta
events.text: Inspired by Bombay's, a dhobi ghat was built in Calcutta (now Kolkata) in 1902. 'Dhobi ghat' is used all over India for any place where many washers work.
events.why: The trade of washing and pressing grew with India's cities.

events.title: A steam pressing machine for tailors
events.text: A tailor designed a foot-operated steam pressing machine for tailors, garment factories and dry cleaners, to replace heavy hand-held steam irons, and a businessman put it into production. The company began in Syracuse in 1904; by the 1930s its successor was one of the largest US makers of laundry and dry-cleaning machines.
events.why: Pressing with steam from a boiler became the way laundries and tailors work.

events.title: The iron with the hot point
events.text: Earl Richardson, a meter reader, persuaded his power company to run electricity all day on Tuesdays, ironing day, so people could use his electric irons. His wife Mary suggested more heat at the tip, for buttonholes and pleats, and laundresses refused to give the new irons back. In 1905 he sold more electric irons than any other company in America, under the name 'Hotpoint'.
events.why: Putting the heat where the work is, at the point, made the electric iron popular.

events.title: The first temperature settings
events.text: The first electric irons had no thermostats. Temperature settings first appeared in 1917.
events.why: An iron that could not hold a temperature scorched cloth easily.

events.title: The first steam iron on sale
events.text: The first commercially available electric steam iron was introduced in 1926 by Eldec, a New York drying and cleaning company. It was not a commercial success.
events.why: It put the laundry's steam into a household iron for the first time.

events.title: The automatic thermostat iron
events.text: Joseph W. Myers, later head of research at Proctor Electric, developed an automatic, adjustable temperature-control iron in the 1920s. Museums date the truly automatic adjustable thermostat iron to 1927.
events.why: A bimetal thermostat lets one iron suit silk, wool and cotton: the dial on every iron today.

events.title: A patent for a steam iron and dampener
events.text: Max Skolnik of Chicago was granted a patent for an electric steam iron and dampener.
events.why: It led to the first steam iron that sold well.

events.title: Steam irons catch on
events.who: Max Skolnik and the Steam-O-Matic Corporation
events.text: Skolnik granted the Steam-O-Matic Corporation of New York the right to make his steam-electric irons: the first steam iron to achieve any real popularity. Steam irons spread in the 1940s and 1950s.
events.why: Steam at home meant no more sprinkling clothes before ironing.

events.title: Twenty million irons from one plant
events.who: Hotpoint, by then part of General Electric
events.text: The Ontario plant presented its 20 millionth iron, gold-plated, to Earl Richardson's sister. The 50 millionth followed in 1956, the 100 millionth in 1969 and the 150 millionth in 1980; the plant closed in 1982.
events.why: The electric iron had become one of the most common machines in the home.

events.title: Care-label symbols
events.text: The international textile care labelling association GINETEX was founded and introduced its care symbols, including the iron with one, two or three dots. Working with ISO, they became the standard ISO 3758.
events.why: The dots tell you how hot the iron may be: up to 110, 150 or 200 °C.

events.title: The ISI mark becomes compulsory for irons in India
events.text: Electric irons were listed for compulsory ISI marking under India's Electrical Wires, Cables, Appliances and Protection Devices and Accessories (Quality Control) Order, 2003, to the safety standard IS 302-2-3.
events.why: Every electric iron sold in India must now be certified to a safety standard.

events.title: A solar ironing cart
events.text: At 14, Vinisha Umashankar designed a solar-powered ironing cart to replace the charcoal irons that press clothes for millions of Indians each day: five hours of sunshine runs the iron for six hours. It made her a finalist for the first Earthshot Prize.
events.why: It keeps the istri-wala's trade and removes the charcoal smoke.

events.title: The care-label standard is revised
events.text: ISO 3758 was revised again in 2023; the new edition adds a symbol for ironing without steam.
events.why: Some fabrics are harmed by steam, so the label can now say so.

events.title: India adopts the latest iron safety standard
events.text: BIS published IS 302 (Part 2/Sec 3):2024, the safety standard for electric irons, identical to the international IEC 60335-2-3:2022. It covers dry and steam irons, including those with a separate boiler.
events.why: Indian irons are tested to the same safety rules as the rest of the world's.
